entry.content:
Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

Part 1 built one attention head from scratch. It ended with two problems:

  1. Attention can’t tell word order. “The cat sat on the mat” and “mat the on sat cat the” look the same to it.
  2. One head can only ask one kind of question at a time.

The paper solves the first with positional encodings and the second with multi-head attention. Both are small ideas. Let’s see them with real numbers.

As before, this is the tiny model from part 1: 8 numbers per word and real arithmetic. The sentence is editable, and scrolling inside a step plays it.

Positions and heads, step by step

First, the problem. On the left is the output of an attention layer for our sentence. On the right is the same sentence reversed.

Every line joins a word to the same word in the other sentence. Their rows are exactly equal. The layer has no idea the order changed. It only moved the rows around.

That makes sense. Attention compares every word with every other word, and nothing in those comparisons says where a word is.

The fix: give each position its own fingerprint. The paper uses waves. Column \(2i\) of the encoding is a sine wave and column \(2i+1\) is a cosine, each at its own speed:

\[PE_{(pos,\,2i)} = \sin\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\] \[PE_{(pos,\,2i+1)} = \cos\!\left(\frac{pos}{10000^{2i/d}}\right)\]

The first pair of waves wiggles fast and the last pair barely moves. Read down at any position (the blue line) and you get 8 heights. That is the position’s row of PE. No two positions have the same row.

Then we simply add. Each word’s row of X gets its position’s row of PE added to it, number by number.

Adding, not appending, keeps the size at 8 numbers. The word is still in there, and now the position is too. Two copies of the at positions 0 and 4 now get different rows.

From here on, every layer sees \(X + PE\) instead of X.

Run the same test again, this time with positions added.

Now the lines turn red and dashed: the same word gets a different output depending on where it stands. Word order finally matters.

(There is nothing special about reversing. Any other order would show the same thing.)

Why waves, and not just the numbers 0, 1, 2, …? Plain counting grows without limit, and the network would only ever see small numbers while training.

Waves stay between −1 and 1. They also have a nice property. Treat each sine/cosine pair as a point on a circle. Moving one position later turns the point by the same angle, wherever it starts.

So “the word just before me” is the same rotation at position 3 as at position 300. A weight matrix can learn to recognise it once and use it everywhere. (The proof is below.) The paper says the authors chose waves because they hoped the model could “easily learn to attend by relative positions”.

Now the second problem. sat wants to know who sat, but also where. One softmax row can’t put most of its weight on two places at once.

So the Transformer runs several heads side by side. Each head has its own \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\) and runs its own attention, exactly as in part 1.

Our toy has 2 heads. Head 1 is the hand-wired one from part 1. Head 2 is random. Hover or tap a row to compare them. In a trained model every head learns a pattern of its own. Some track the previous word, some link a pronoun to its noun, and some just look at punctuation.

Each head is made smaller, so the total cost stays the same. With \(d_{model} = 8\) and 2 heads, each head works with \(d_k = 8 / 2 = 4\) numbers.

The heads’ outputs are placed side by side (“concatenated”) to get back to 8 numbers per word. Then one more matrix, \(W_O\), mixes them. The square brackets mean “side by side”:

\[\text{MultiHead}(X) = [\,\text{head}_1 \cdots \text{head}_h\,]\, W_O\]

The paper uses 8 heads of 64 numbers each: \(8 \times 64 = 512 = d_{model}\).

Was it worth it? The paper compares attention with recurrent layers. Drag the slider to change the number of words.

Attention compares every pair of words, so its work grows like \(n^2\). A recurrent layer does less work per word for long inputs, but it has to go one word after another: \(n\) steps, each waiting for the last.

For sentences shorter than \(d\) (512 in the paper), attention is both cheaper and fully parallel. That speed is a big part of why Transformers took over. The \(n^2\) cost for very long texts is why so much later research tries to make attention cheaper.

What we have so far

We now have the full multi-head attention sublayer of the paper:

  1. Add positions: \(X \leftarrow X + PE\).
  2. For each head h: \(\text{head}_h = \text{Attention}(X W_Q^h,\; X W_K^h,\; X W_V^h)\).
  3. Join the heads and mix: \(\text{Concat}(\text{head}_1, \ldots, \text{head}_h)\, W_O\).

Its output has the same shape as its input: one row of \(d_{model}\) numbers per word. The paper draws it as its Figure 2 (right). Drag the slider to change the number of heads, with the paper’s \(d_{model} = 512\):

One detail I glossed over: the paper also multiplies the embeddings by \(\sqrt{d_{model}}\) before adding positions, so the two have similar sizes. In this toy the embeddings already have about the right size, so I left that out.

Attention lets words share information, but it doesn’t do much with that information on its own. In part 3 we wrap it in the rest of an encoder block: residual connections, layer normalisation and a small feed-forward network.

Going deeper

Why a shift is a rotation

Take one sine/cosine pair with speed \(\omega\). Write \(a = \omega p\) for the angle at position \(p\), and \(b = \omega k\) for the extra angle after \(k\) more steps. The angle-addition rules say:

\[\sin(a + b) = \sin a \cos b + \cos a \sin b\] \[\cos(a + b) = \cos a \cos b - \sin a \sin b\]

In matrix form:

\[\begin{pmatrix} \sin(a+b) \\ \cos(a+b) \end{pmatrix} = \begin{pmatrix} \cos b & \sin b \\ -\sin b & \cos b \end{pmatrix} \begin{pmatrix} \sin a \\ \cos a \end{pmatrix}\]

The matrix in the middle is a rotation by the angle \(b = \omega k\). It depends on \(k\) but not on \(p\). So “\(k\) places later” is the same fixed matrix at every position. A weight matrix like \(W_Q\) multiplies by fixed matrices, so in principle it can learn “the word just before me” once and have it work everywhere.

Dot products only see distance

Here’s another consequence. Take the dot product of two position rows, \(PE(p)\) and \(PE(p+k)\). Each sine/cosine pair contributes \(\sin a \sin b + \cos a \cos b = \cos(a - b)\), so

\[PE(p) \cdot PE(p+k) = \sum_i \cos(\omega_i k)\]

This depends only on the distance \(k\), not on where you are. In our toy (\(d = 8\)), positions 3 apart always have a dot product of 1.96, whether they are positions 0 and 3 or 40 and 43.

It’s also the same for \(+k\) and \(-k\), since cosine doesn’t care about sign. On their own, the dot products can’t tell “3 words before” from “3 words after”. The rotation above can, which is one reason the learned \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) matter.

Why add the positions, and not append them?

Appending would give each word \([x,\ p]\): twice as many numbers. But the first thing the layer does is multiply by a matrix. Split that matrix into a top half \(W_a\) (for the word) and a bottom half \(W_b\) (for the position):

\[[x,\ p] \begin{pmatrix} W_a \\ W_b \end{pmatrix} = x W_a + p W_b\]

So appending and then multiplying is the same as adding a transformed position. Adding the position directly is the special case \(W_b = W_a\), and it saves the extra width. In 512 dimensions there is plenty of room for the model to keep word and position information in different directions, so little is lost.

What a score sees once positions are added

With positions added, the score between word \(i\) and word \(j\) is \((x_i + p_i)\, A\, (x_j + p_j)^\top\), where \(A = W_Q W_K^\top\) as in part 1. Multiply out the brackets:

\[\underbrace{x_i A x_j^\top}_{\text{word–word}} + \underbrace{x_i A p_j^\top}_{\text{word–position}} + \underbrace{p_i A x_j^\top}_{\text{position–word}} + \underbrace{p_i A p_j^\top}_{\text{position–position}}\]

Each term asks a different question. The first is the content match from part 1. The last depends only on the two positions: “look one word back” lives here. The middle two mix the two: “the word at the start of the sentence”. One matrix \(A\) has to serve all four. Transformer-XL took this expansion as its starting point, and gave the position terms their own weights, using only the distance \(i - j\).

Why 10000, and why so many speeds?

The speeds are \(\omega_i = 1 / 10000^{2i/d}\), so the wavelengths grow geometrically from \(2\pi\) (about 6 positions) to \(10000 \cdot 2\pi\) (about 63,000 positions).

Think of the hands of a clock. The fast hand tells neighbouring positions apart, but it repeats every few steps. The slow hands barely move between neighbours, but they tell far-apart positions apart. Together, every position gets a unique pattern, and 10000 makes the slowest wave far longer than any sentence the model will see.

Learned positions work too

The paper also tried simply learning a vector for each position, like a second embedding table. The results were nearly identical (Table 3, row E). The authors kept the waves because they hoped the model could then handle sentences longer than any it saw in training.

Later models went both ways. BERT and GPT-2 learned their positions. Many of today’s models use RoPE (Su et al., 2021), which takes the rotation above literally: it rotates each query and key by its position, so a score depends only on the distance between the two words.

RoPE in one line

RoPE rotates the query of the word at position \(m\) by \(R_m\) (a rotation by \(m\omega\), as above) and the key at position \(n\) by \(R_n\). Their score is

\[(q R_m)\cdot(k R_n) = q\, R_m R_n^\top\, k^\top = q\, R_{m-n}\, k^\top\]

using two facts about rotations: undoing a rotation is rotating backwards (\(R_n^\top = R_{-n}\)), and two rotations add their angles (\(R_m R_{-n} = R_{m-n}\)). Only the distance \(m - n\) is left. Unlike the added waves, nothing about the absolute position survives in the score, and unlike plain dot products of positions, \(R_{m-n}\) and \(R_{n-m}\) differ, so before and after are told apart.

Deriving RoPE from what we want

The line above checks that rotation works. Su et al. (2021, section 3.4) go the other way: they start from the property we want and show that rotation is the answer. Here is that argument for one pair of numbers.

Set up. Treat a 2-number vector \((a, b)\) as the complex number \(a + ib\), where \(i = \sqrt{-1}\) (so in this section and the next, \(i\) is never an index). Then the dot product of two such vectors is the real part of one times the conjugate of the other: \((a, b) \cdot (c, d) = \text{Re}\big[(a + ib)(c - id)\big]\). We look for a way \(f(q, m)\) to mark a query \(q\) with its position \(m\) (and the same \(f\) for keys), such that

\[f(q, m)\; \overline{f(k, n)} = g(q, k, m - n) \qquad \text{and} \qquad f(x, 0) = x\]

The first condition says the product, and so the score, depends on the positions only through their distance. The second says position 0 leaves a vector alone.

Step 1: polar form. Write each complex number as a length and an angle: \(f(q, m) = r(q, m)\, e^{i \Theta(q, m)}\). Multiplying complex numbers multiplies lengths and adds angles (the conjugate flips the sign of an angle), so the condition splits in two:

\[r(q, m)\, r(k, n) = r_g(q, k, m - n), \qquad \Theta(q, m) - \Theta(k, n) = \Theta_g(q, k, m - n)\]

Step 2: lengths don’t move. Set \(n = m\), so the distance is 0. The right side no longer depends on \(m\), so it equals its value at \(m = 0\), where \(f(x, 0) = x\):

\[r(q, m)\, r(k, m) = r(q, 0)\, r(k, 0) = \lVert q\rVert\, \lVert k\rVert\]

The simplest solution, and the one RoPE uses, is \(r(q, m) = \lVert q \rVert\): marking a vector with its position never changes its length.

Step 3: every vector turns by the same amount. Do the same with the angles. Let \(\theta_q\) and \(\theta_k\) be the original angles of \(q\) and \(k\). With \(n = m\),

\[\Theta(q, m) - \Theta(k, m) = \theta_q - \theta_k \quad\Rightarrow\quad \Theta(q, m) - \theta_q = \Theta(k, m) - \theta_k\]

The left side involves only \(q\) and the right only \(k\), and they are equal for every \(q\) and \(k\). So both are some function of the position alone. Call it \(\phi(m)\): each vector is turned by \(\phi(m)\) at position \(m\), whatever it is.

Step 4: the turn grows in equal steps. Now set \(n = m - 1\), a distance of 1. The angle condition becomes

\[\big(\theta_q + \phi(m)\big) - \big(\theta_k + \phi(m-1)\big) = \Theta_g(q, k, 1)\]

so \(\phi(m) - \phi(m-1) = \Theta_g(q, k, 1) - \theta_q + \theta_k\), which does not depend on \(m\). A function that goes up by the same amount \(\omega\) at every step is a straight line, \(\phi(m) = m\omega + \phi(0)\), and \(f(x, 0) = x\) forces \(\phi(0) = 0\).

Result. Putting the length and the angle back together:

\[f(q, m) = \lVert q \rVert\, e^{i(\theta_q + m\omega)} = q\, e^{i m \omega}\]

Multiplying by \(e^{im\omega}\) is rotating by \(m\omega\). So once we ask for “distance only” and “position 0 does nothing” (plus the simple choice of length in step 2), rotation is the only answer. With \(d\) numbers, RoPE does this for each of the \(d/2\) pairs, with speeds \(\omega_l = 10000^{-2l/d}\), the same as the sinusoidal waves. The EleutherAI write-up walks through the same steps with code.

Do far-apart words matter less under RoPE?

Write the score as a sum over the \(d/2\) pairs. With \(h_l = q_{[l]}\, \overline{k_{[l]}}\) for pair \(l\) (as complex numbers) and distance \(r = m - n\):

\[\text{score} = \text{Re} \sum_{l=0}^{d/2 - 1} h_l\, e^{i r \omega_l}\]

Su et al. bound this with Abel summation, the sum version of integration by parts. Let \(S_0 = 0\) and \(S_j = \sum_{l < j} e^{i r \omega_l}\), so \(e^{i r \omega_l} = S_{l+1} - S_l\), and set \(h_{d/2} = 0\). Then, regrouping the terms,

\[\sum_l h_l (S_{l+1} - S_l) = -\sum_{j=1}^{d/2} S_j\, (h_j - h_{j-1}) \quad\Rightarrow\quad \lvert \text{score} \rvert \le \Big(\max_j \lvert h_j - h_{j-1} \rvert\Big) \sum_{j=1}^{d/2} \lvert S_j \rvert\]

The first factor depends only on \(q\) and \(k\). The second depends only on the distance \(r\), so it is a ceiling on how much any pair of vectors can score at that distance. For \(d = 128\), the average of \(\lvert S_j \rvert\) comes out at:

distance \(r\) 0 10 100 1000 4000
average \(\lvert S_j \rvert\) 32.5 18.0 10.2 4.5 5.0

The ceiling trends down as words get further apart, with some wiggles. Two caveats keep this honest. The decay is computed, not proved: the paper shows the same curve as a plot. And it is a bound for all possible \(q\) and \(k\), often far above the real score; a trained head can still look a thousand words back if its query and key line up.

Why one head can’t look at two places

Row \(i\) of a head’s weights is a set of positive numbers adding up to 1, so the output for word \(i\) is a weighted average of the value rows:

\[o_i = \sum_j P_{ij}\, v_j, \qquad P_{ij} \ge 0, \quad \sum_j P_{ij} = 1\]

Suppose sat needs both cat’s value and mat’s. The best one head can do is split its weight, say \(\lambda\) and \(1 - \lambda\), and return the blend \(\lambda v_{cat} + (1-\lambda) v_{mat}\). Both are in there, but mixed into the same numbers, and the more it gets of one, the less it gets of the other.

Two heads don’t have to share. Head 1 puts all its weight on cat, head 2 on mat, and the concatenation keeps the two values in separate columns. The next matrix, \(W_O\), sees each one whole.

Concat, then W_O, is a sum over heads

Cut \(W_O\) into \(h\) horizontal slices, one per head, each \(d_k \times d_{model}\). Multiplying a row of blocks by a column of blocks works block by block, so

\[[\,\text{head}_1 \cdots \text{head}_h\,] \begin{pmatrix} W_O^{(1)} \\ \vdots \\ W_O^{(h)} \end{pmatrix} = \sum_{k=1}^{h} \text{head}_k\, W_O^{(k)}\]

So “concatenate and mix” is the same as letting every head write its own contribution, through its own matrix, and adding them up. Nothing in the layer makes heads talk to each other. That is what lets researchers study one head at a time (Elhage et al., 2021).

Where the paper’s Table 1 comes from

The paper’s case for attention (section 4) is a table comparing layer types, for \(n\) words of \(d\) numbers each. Each entry is a count you can do by hand:

layer work per layer steps that must wait longest path between two words
self-attention \(O(n^2 d)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(1)\)
recurrent \(O(n d^2)\) \(O(n)\) \(O(n)\)
convolution, width \(k\) \(O(k\, n\, d^2)\) \(O(1)\) \(O(\log_k n)\)
  • Self-attention. \(QK^\top\) is \(n^2\) dot products of length \(d\). All of them are independent, so nothing waits. Every word reads every word directly, so any two are one step apart.
  • Recurrent. Each step computes \(h_t = f(h_{t-1} W + x_t U)\): a \(d \times d\) matrix times a vector, \(d^2\) work, done \(n\) times. Step \(t\) needs step \(t-1\), so there are \(n\) waits. Information from word 1 reaches word \(n\) after \(n\) steps.
  • Convolution. Each output reads \(k\) neighbours through a \(d \times d\) matrix each: \(k d^2\) per word. One layer only reaches \(k\) words, so joining two far-apart words takes a stack: \(O(n/k)\) layers, or \(O(\log_k n)\) with dilated convolutions.

Compare the first two: attention is cheaper exactly when \(n^2 d < n d^2\), that is when \(n < d\). With \(d = 512\), that held for most sentences in 2017. The last column is the deeper argument. A short path means a gradient from one word reaches another in one hop, which the paper argues makes long-range patterns easier to learn.

Many heads cost the same as one

Each head has its own \(W_Q\), \(W_K\) and \(W_V\), each of size \(d \times (d/h)\). Over \(h\) heads that is \(3 \cdot h \cdot d \cdot (d/h) = 3d^2\) weights, plus \(d^2\) for \(W_O\):

\[4d^2 \text{ weights, whatever } h \text{ is.}\]

So splitting into heads is free. The paper tested this (Table 3, row A). One big head scored 0.9 BLEU worse than 8 heads. Too many heads hurt as well: with 32 heads of size 16, quality dropped again. Each head needs enough numbers to ask a useful question.

Part 1’s rank argument says why. A head of size \(d_k = d/h\) can only make every possible pattern over \(n\) words if \(d_k \ge n\), that is \(h \le d/n\). Bhojanapalli et al. (2020) checked this in BERT-large (\(d = 1024\), sequences of \(n = 128\), so the limit is \(h = 8\)), keeping the weight count fixed at 336 million:

heads head size \(d_k\) SQuAD F1 MNLI accuracy
8 128 90.89 85.0
16 64 90.61 84.5
32 32 90.45 84.4

Past 8 heads, each head drops below \(n\) and scores slip. The drop is small, but it goes one way. Their fix is to stop tying the head size to \(d/h\): pick \(d_k\) by itself, at least as big as \(n\). “Free” is true for the weight count, not for what each head can express.

Further reading

  • Vaswani et al., Attention Is All You Need, sections 3.2.2 (multi-head), 3.5 (positions) and 4 (why self-attention).
  • Amirhossein Kazemnejad, Transformer Architecture: The Positional Encoding: a careful look at the rotation property.
  • Jesse Vig, BertViz: see what real attention heads learn.
  • Su et al., RoFormer: Enhanced Transformer with Rotary Position Embedding (2021): section 3.4 has the derivation and the decay bound.
  • Biderman et al., Rotary Embeddings: A Relative Revolution (EleutherAI, 2021): RoPE derived with complex numbers, plus experiments.
  • Lilian Weng, The Transformer Family Version 2.0 (2023): a survey of position encodings and attention variants.

Series · Attention is all you need 1Self-attention from scratch 2Multi-head attention and positions 3One encoder block 4The decoder, masking and training 5Inference and the KV cache

In 2017 a team at Google published a paper with a bold title: Attention Is All You Need. It described the Transformer. Today almost every large language model, from ChatGPT to Claude, is built on it.

This series rebuilds the Transformer piece by piece. Every figure runs a real (but tiny) Transformer in your browser, and every number you see is computed, not drawn by hand. You can change the sentence and watch every matrix change with it.

This first part covers the idea at the heart of the paper: self-attention. In a previous post I treated the network as a black box that hands out scores. Now we open the box.

The toy model

Real models are huge: GPT-3 gives each word 12,288 numbers. Ours gives each word 8, so whole matrices fit on screen. The rest of the setup:

  • a vocabulary of about 30 words (press words it knows in the figure to see them),
  • attention with d_k = 4 numbers per query and key,
  • weights from a fixed random seed, except for one attention head that I wired by hand so it has a clear story to tell.

The model is not trained, so it can’t write a sentence. But the arithmetic is exactly the arithmetic of the paper. I checked it against PyTorch’s own Transformer layers, and they agree to within 10⁻¹⁴.

Self-attention, step by step

Before Transformers, language models were mostly recurrent networks (RNNs). They read a sentence like we do: one word at a time, left to right.

After each word, the RNN updates one memory vector, h. Everything it knows about the start of the sentence has to survive being passed down that chain.

Two problems follow. Long sentences get blurry, because early words fade from the memory. And it is slow, because word 6 can’t start until word 5 is done.

Attention throws the chain away. Every word gets to look straight at every other word, in one step.

The distance between the first and the last word is now the same as between neighbours: one hop. And all the pairs can be computed at the same time, which is what GPUs are good at.

The question is how much each word should look at each other word. That is what the next steps compute.

First, words become numbers. Each word in the vocabulary has an id, and the embedding table E has one row per id. We look up one row per word and stack them into a matrix X.

X has one row per word and 8 columns. In a real model the columns are learned and mean nothing we can name. In this toy I gave them names: noun, verb, animal, and so on. That makes it easier to see why the attention below comes out the way it does.

Each word asks a question. We multiply X by a weight matrix \(W_Q\) to get the queries \(Q = X W_Q\).

Watch the figure: row i of X times column j of \(W_Q\) gives cell (i, j) of Q. Multiply the pairs and add them up, as written at the bottom of the figure. That is all matrix multiplication is.

The wiring I chose means a verb’s query says “I’m looking for an animal” and a preposition’s query says “I’m looking for a thing”.

Two more matrices, the same trick. \(K = X W_K\) gives every word a key, and \(V = X W_V\) gives it a value.

A helpful picture is a library search:

  • the query is what you type into the search box,
  • each key is the label on a book’s spine,
  • each value is what is inside the book.

Queries are matched against keys. Values are what you take home.

Now we score every pair. The score for word i looking at word j is the dot product of query i and key j. Doing all pairs at once is one matrix product: \(Q K^\top\).

\(K^\top\) is K turned on its side, so its columns are the keys. The result is a square grid: one row per word asking, one column per word being asked.

A large dot product means the query and the key point the same way: a good match. Red cells are strong matches.

Then we shrink the scores, dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\). With \(d_k = 4\), that is a divide by 2.

Why? A dot product adds up \(d_k\) products. The more terms, the bigger the scores get (they grow like \(\sqrt{d_k}\)). Very big scores make the next step, softmax, put almost all the weight on one word. Then learning gets stuck.

Try the demo on the right. Random queries and keys, with \(d_k\) = 1024 and no division, hand nearly 100% to one word. Tick divide by √d_k and the spread comes back.

Where does \(\sqrt{d_k}\) come from? See why divide by √d_k further down.

Scores become weights. We apply softmax to each row. It makes every number positive and makes each row add up to exactly 1:

\[\text{softmax}(x)_i = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}\]

Now row i says how word i splits its attention: a percentage for every word in the sentence. Hover or tap a row label to see it as bars.

Look at sat: most of its attention goes to cat. The verb found who did the sitting.

Finally, we mix the values. Multiply the weights by V. Output row i is a blend of all the value rows, each in the amount given by row i of the weights.

So the new vector for sat is mostly cat’s value, plus a little of everything else. Each word has gathered information from the words that matter to it.

The output has one row per word, just like X. That’s important: it means we can stack these layers, as part 3 shows.

Here is the whole head at a glance. Each line goes from a word asking (left) to a word being asked (right). Thicker lines mean more attention.

Hover a word on the left. Then try your own sentence in the box above: “the quick brown fox jumped over the lazy dog” or “my dog chased a ball in the park”.

Adjectives find their nouns, verbs find animals, prepositions find things. In a trained model nobody wires this by hand. It is learned from data, and some heads really do learn patterns like these.

The whole thing in one line

Everything the figure did is the paper’s equation (1):

\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{Q K^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) V\]

with \(Q = X W_Q\), \(K = X W_K\) and \(V = X W_V\). Reading it from the inside out:

  1. \(Q K^\top\): score every query against every key.
  2. \(\div \sqrt{d_k}\): keep the scores in a sensible range.
  3. softmax: turn each row of scores into weights that sum to 1.
  4. \(\times V\): mix the values with those weights.

The paper draws the same four steps as a flow chart, its Figure 2 (left). Here it is again, with the shape of every matrix written on its arrow:

Every shape follows from the rules of matrix multiplication: an \(a \times b\) matrix times a \(b \times c\) matrix gives \(a \times c\). With \(n\) words:

matrix shape in our toy
\(X\) \(n \times d_{model}\) 6 × 8
\(W_Q,\ W_K,\ W_V\) \(d_{model} \times d_k\) 8 × 4
\(Q,\ K,\ V\) \(n \times d_k\) 6 × 4
\(Q K^\top\) and its softmax \(n \times n\) 6 × 6
output \(n \times d_k\) 6 × 4

Counting the multiply-adds gives the cost: \(3\, n\, d_{model}\, d_k\) for the three projections, then \(n^2 d_k\) for \(Q K^\top\) and another \(n^2 d_k\) for the mix with \(V\). The first part grows like \(n\), the second like \(n^2\). Part 2 comes back to that square.

It is called scaled dot-product attention. It is self-attention when queries, keys and values all come from the same sentence, as here. In part 4 we’ll meet cross-attention, where the queries come from one sentence and the keys and values from another.

What’s still missing

Two things in our figure should bother you.

  • Word order. Nothing in these steps knows where a word is. Shuffle the sentence and each word gets exactly the same output, just in a different row. (Try “mat the on sat cat the”, or read the proof.)
  • One question per word. A single head can only look for one kind of thing at a time. sat wants to know who sat and where.

The paper fixes both, with positional encodings and multi-head attention. That is part 2.

Going deeper

The steps above show what happens. This section is about why. Each question stands on its own, so skip to the ones you care about.

Why divide by √d_k?

Picture a fresh model, before any training. Its weights are random, so the numbers in each query and key behave like independent random numbers with mean 0 and variance 1.

A score is a dot product: \(q \cdot k = q_1 k_1 + q_2 k_2 + \dots + q_{d_k} k_{d_k}\).

Work out the mean and variance of one term, \(q_i k_i\). Because \(q_i\) and \(k_i\) are independent, the average of a product is the product of the averages:

\[\mathbb{E}[q_i k_i] = \mathbb{E}[q_i]\,\mathbb{E}[k_i] = 0 \cdot 0 = 0\] \[\text{Var}(q_i k_i) = \mathbb{E}[q_i^2 k_i^2] - \big(\mathbb{E}[q_i k_i]\big)^2 = \mathbb{E}[q_i^2]\,\mathbb{E}[k_i^2] - 0 = 1 \cdot 1 = 1\]

(For a mean-0 number, \(\mathbb{E}[q_i^2]\) is its variance, which is 1.) Different terms are independent too, so their variances simply add:

\[\text{Var}(q \cdot k) = \sum_{i=1}^{d_k} \text{Var}(q_i k_i) = d_k\]

So the typical size of a score, its standard deviation, is \(\sqrt{d_k}\). Dividing a number by \(c\) divides its variance by \(c^2\), so

\[\text{Var}\!\left(\frac{q \cdot k}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right) = \frac{d_k}{d_k} = 1\]

whatever \(d_k\) is.

This is footnote 4 of the paper. With the paper’s \(d_k = 64\), raw scores are typically around ±8. Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) brings the spread back to about 1, whatever \(d_k\) is.

Try it below. The left panel keeps a fixed axis, so you can watch the raw scores spread out as \(d_k\) grows. The right panel, after dividing, keeps the same shape.

Why a big spread is bad. Softmax turns scores into weights. Its gradient says how much weight \(p_i\) moves when score \(x_j\) moves. Write \(Z = \sum_l e^{x_l}\) for the bottom of the fraction, so \(p_i = e^{x_i} / Z\) and \(\partial Z / \partial x_j = e^{x_j}\). The quotient rule gives

\[\frac{\partial p_i}{\partial x_j} = \frac{\delta_{ij}\, e^{x_i} Z - e^{x_i} e^{x_j}}{Z^2} = \frac{e^{x_i}}{Z}\left(\delta_{ij} - \frac{e^{x_j}}{Z}\right) = p_i\,(\delta_{ij} - p_j)\]

where \(\delta_{ij}\) is 1 if \(i = j\) and 0 otherwise. As a matrix, the whole Jacobian is \(\text{diag}(p) - p\,p^\top\).

Now suppose the winner has weight \(1 - \varepsilon\), so all the others share \(\varepsilon\). Then every entry is at most \(\varepsilon\):

  • for the winner’s own entry, \(p_i(1 - p_i) = (1 - \varepsilon)\,\varepsilon \le \varepsilon\);
  • any other entry in the winner’s row is \(p_i p_j \le p_j \le \varepsilon\);
  • every other row starts with a factor \(p_i \le \varepsilon\).

So as the softmax approaches one-hot, its whole gradient goes to 0, as fast as \(\varepsilon\) does.

So almost no gradient flows back to \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\), and attention stops learning. In the paper’s words, large dot products “push the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients”. The table in the figure measures this: at \(d_k = 1024\) without the division, the top word takes about 98% and the gradient is more than ten times smaller than with it.

One caveat: the “independent, variance 1” picture is exact only at the start of training. Trained queries and keys are not random. But the start is exactly where it matters. A model that can’t take its first steps never learns anything.

Why not divide by d_k?

That over-corrects. The spread would become \(1/\sqrt{d_k}\): about 0.125 for \(d_k = 64\). Scores that small make the softmax nearly flat, so every word gets about the same weight and attention can’t pick anything out. \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is the one divisor that keeps the spread at 1 for every size.

There is a twist. After training, queries and keys are no longer independent, and their dot products can grow like \(d_k\) rather than \(\sqrt{d_k}\). For that reason, some recipes for very wide models (μP, Yang et al., 2022) do divide by \(d_k\).

A dot product, or a small network?

Before the Transformer, the popular choice was additive attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014). It scores a pair with a tiny neural network, \(v^\top \tanh(W_1 q + W_2 k)\), instead of a dot product.

The paper says the two work about equally well in theory, but dot products are much faster, because all the scores come out of one matrix multiplication. It also notes that without scaling, additive attention beat dot-product attention for larger \(d_k\). The authors suspected the large-dot-product problem above, which is why they added the \(\sqrt{d_k}\).

Why two matrices, W_Q and W_K?

Write \(x_i\) for word \(i\)’s row of \(X\). Its score against word \(j\) is

\[q_i \cdot k_j = (x_i W_Q)(x_j W_K)^\top = x_i \,\big(W_Q W_K^\top\big)\, x_j^\top\]

So a head really uses one \(d_{model} \times d_{model}\) matrix, \(A = W_Q W_K^\top\). Storing it as two thin factors has two benefits. It takes \(2\, d_{model}\, d_k\) numbers instead of \(d_{model}^2\). (In our toy the two happen to be equal, 64 each. For one head of the paper’s model it is 65,536 instead of 262,144.) And it caps the rank of \(A\) at \(d_k\): one head can only compare words along \(d_k\) directions, which is part of why it can only ask one kind of question.

Why not one matrix W for both queries and keys? Then \(A = W W^\top\) and the score of word i looking at word j would be \(x_i W W^\top x_j^\top\), which is exactly the score of j looking at i. Every score grid would be symmetric. (The weights need not be, since each row is softmaxed on its own, but a big score from i to j would always mean a big score back.)

Language isn’t symmetric. In our hand-wired head, sat looks hard at cat (score 1.92), but cat barely looks at sat (score 0.02). The verb is searching for its subject; the noun isn’t searching for its verb. Separate \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) let “what I’m looking for” differ from “what I offer”.

Can one head make any pattern?

The rank cap above has a sharp consequence. Bhojanapalli et al. (2020) asked: given \(n\) words, can one head produce any \(n \times n\) weight matrix \(P\) we like (positive entries, rows adding to 1)? The answer depends on whether \(d_k \ge n\).

When \(d_k \ge n\), yes. Take \(X\) with \(n\) independent rows (so \(d_{model} \ge n\)). Then it has a right inverse \(X^+\) with \(X X^+ = I_n\). We want scores \(S = \log P\), because then \(\text{softmax}(S)\) is \(P\) back again: each row of \(e^{\log P}\) already adds to 1. So pick

\[W_Q W_K^\top = \sqrt{d_k}\; X^+ (\log P)\, (X^+)^\top\]

and check it, step by step:

\[S = \frac{X\, W_Q W_K^\top X^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}} = (X X^+)\,(\log P)\,(X X^+)^\top = I \cdot \log P \cdot I = \log P\]

The middle matrix has rank at most \(n \le d_k\), so it really can be split into two \(d_{model} \times d_k\) factors.

When \(d_k < n\), not always. The scores \(S\) have rank at most \(d_k\). Softmax ignores a constant added to a row, so the scores that produce \(P\) are exactly \(\log P + c\,\mathbf{1}^\top\) for some column \(c\). Adding \(c\,\mathbf{1}^\top\) is adding a rank-1 matrix, which changes the rank by at most 1. So if \(\text{rank}(\log P) > d_k + 1\), no choice of weights reaches \(P\).

The rank count is not the only way to fail. Even when it allows a pattern, the embeddings themselves can block it. The smallest case: let \(d_{model} = d_k = 1\) and \(n = 2\), with word 1 embedded as \(x_1 = 1\) and word 2 as \(x_2 = 0\). Every score is \(x_i\, w\, x_j / 1\), so

\[S = \begin{pmatrix} w & 0 \\ 0 & 0 \end{pmatrix}, \qquad \text{softmax}(\text{row } 2) = (0.5,\ 0.5) \text{ for every } w\]

Word 2’s embedding is 0, so all its scores are 0 and it can never prefer anyone, whatever the weights. Part 2 shows what this means for splitting a model into many small heads.

Why softmax?

We want weights that are positive and add up to 1, so the output is a weighted average of the values. Softmax gives that, and it is smooth, so gradients can flow through it. Picking only the top word (a “hard” max) has no useful gradient at all.

There is a neater reason, too. Among all ways of splitting weight over the words, softmax is the one that best trades off two wishes: put weight on high scores, and stay spread out. Score a split \(p\) by

\[\sum_i p_i x_i + \tau H(p), \qquad H(p) = -\sum_i p_i \log p_i\]

where \(H\) is the entropy (how spread out \(p\) is) and \(\tau > 0\) says how much spread matters. Maximise it subject to \(\sum_i p_i = 1\) with a Lagrange multiplier \(\lambda\). Setting the derivative with respect to \(p_i\) to zero:

\[x_i - \tau(\log p_i + 1) + \lambda = 0 \quad\Rightarrow\quad p_i = e^{x_i / \tau} \cdot e^{\lambda/\tau - 1}\]

The last factor is the same for every \(i\), and it has to make the weights add up to 1. So \(p_i = e^{x_i/\tau} / \sum_j e^{x_j/\tau}\): exactly the softmax of \(x / \tau\).

\(\tau\) is called the temperature. As \(\tau \to 0\), spread stops mattering and the answer becomes the hard max. As \(\tau \to \infty\), only spread matters and every word gets \(1/n\). Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) is choosing a temperature of \(\sqrt{d_k}\), which is why too small a divisor gives a near-hard max and too big a one a near-flat row.

A handy property: adding the same number \(c\) to every score in a row changes nothing, because it cancels between the top and bottom of the fraction:

\[\frac{e^{x_i + c}}{\sum_j e^{x_j + c}} = \frac{e^c\, e^{x_i}}{e^c \sum_j e^{x_j}} = \frac{e^{x_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_j}}\]

Code uses this to subtract each row’s maximum before taking \(e^x\), so the numbers never overflow. The toy model here does the same.

Attention is one step of a memory lookup

There is a second derivation of the same formula, from memory instead of from weights. Ramsauer et al. (2020) treat the keys \(k_1, \dots, k_n\) as stored memories and a query \(q\) as a noisy cue. To recall the memory that matches the cue, they define an energy that is low near a good match:

\[E(q) = -\,L(q) + \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert q \rVert^2, \qquad L(q) = \frac{1}{\beta} \log \sum_j e^{\beta\, q \cdot k_j}\]

\(L\) is a smooth maximum (“log-sum-exp”) of the scores, so \(-L\) pulls \(q\) toward the best key, and \(\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert q\rVert^2\) stops \(q\) from running off to infinity. \(\beta\) plays the role of \(1/\tau\).

Step 1: the gradient of \(L\) is attention. Differentiate the log, then the sum:

\[\nabla L(q) = \frac{1}{\beta} \cdot \frac{\sum_j \beta\, k_j\, e^{\beta\, q \cdot k_j}}{\sum_j e^{\beta\, q \cdot k_j}} = \sum_j p_j\, k_j, \qquad p = \text{softmax}(\beta\, q K^\top)\]

A softmax-weighted average of the keys.

Step 2: \(L\) is convex. Differentiate once more. The Hessian is \(\beta\, K^\top \big(\text{diag}(p) - p\,p^\top\big) K\), the same softmax Jacobian as in the √d_k section. For any vector \(u\),

\[u^\top \big(\text{diag}(p) - p\,p^\top\big) u = \sum_j p_j u_j^2 - \Big(\sum_j p_j u_j\Big)^2\]

which is the variance of \(u\) under the weights \(p\), so it is never negative.

Step 3: the update. \(E\) is “convex minus convex”. The standard trick for such functions (the concave–convex procedure) is to set the gradient of the convex part at the new point equal to the gradient of the subtracted part at the old point: \(q_{new} = \nabla L(q_{old})\). By step 1,

\[q_{new} = \text{softmax}\big(\beta\, q_{old} K^\top\big)\, K\]

Step 4: the energy never goes up. Because \(L\) is convex, it lies above its tangent line: \(L(q_{new}) \ge L(q_{old}) + q_{new} \cdot (q_{new} - q_{old})\), using \(\nabla L(q_{old}) = q_{new}\). Put that into \(E(q_{new}) - E(q_{old})\):

\[E(q_{new}) - E(q_{old}) \le \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert q_{new}\rVert^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert q_{old}\rVert^2 - q_{new}\cdot q_{new} + q_{new} \cdot q_{old} = -\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert q_{new} - q_{old}\rVert^2 \le 0\]

So every step moves downhill. The paper also shows that when the memories are well separated, one step already lands almost exactly on the nearest one.

Now set \(\beta = 1/\sqrt{d_k}\) and read the stored patterns out through a separate value matrix, \(V\) instead of \(K\). The update becomes \(\text{softmax}(q K^\top / \sqrt{d_k})\, V\): one attention row. A Transformer takes this step once per layer rather than repeating it until it settles, so attention has the same form as a Hopfield update rather than being one in the strict sense. It also explains the temperature from a new angle: a large \(\beta\) (small \(\tau\)) recalls one memory, a small \(\beta\) blends many. The authors’ blog post has pictures.

Why a dot product, and not a distance?

A natural alternative is to score a pair by how close the query and the key are: minus half the squared distance. Expand it:

\[-\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert q - k_j \rVert^2 = q \cdot k_j - \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert q \rVert^2 - \tfrac{1}{2}\lVert k_j \rVert^2\]

The middle term is the same for every key in the row, so by the property above the softmax ignores it. What’s left is the dot product plus a bonus \(-\tfrac{1}{2}\lVert k_j\rVert^2\) for each key. So distance-based attention is dot-product attention with one extra rule: long keys get penalised. The dot product is the simpler of the two, it is one matrix multiply, and \(W_K\) can learn to control key lengths anyway.

Attention as a kernel smoother

Write one output row without matrices:

\[o_i = \frac{\sum_j \kappa(q_i, k_j)\, v_j}{\sum_j \kappa(q_i, k_j)}, \qquad \kappa(q, k) = e^{\,q \cdot k / \tau}\]

Statisticians have used this shape since the 1960s. It is a Nadaraya–Watson kernel smoother: estimate a value at \(q_i\) by averaging the known values \(v_j\), weighted by a kernel \(\kappa\) that says how similar \(q_i\) is to \(k_j\). Tsai et al. (2019) read attention this way and asked which kernel works best.

Run the distance expansion above backwards and the exponential kernel splits into three factors:

\[e^{\,q \cdot k/\tau} = e^{\lVert q\rVert^2 / 2\tau} \cdot e^{\lVert k\rVert^2 / 2\tau} \cdot e^{-\lVert q - k\rVert^2 / 2\tau}\]

The first factor is the same for the whole row, so it cancels between top and bottom. The last is the Gaussian (RBF) kernel, the textbook choice. So softmax attention is a Gaussian kernel smoother in which each key also carries a weight \(e^{\lVert k\rVert^2/2\tau}\).

Tsai et al. swapped the kernel in a Transformer for translation and compared BLEU (higher is better):

Kernel \(\kappa(q, k)\) BLEU
linear, \(q \cdot k\) did not train
polynomial, \((q \cdot k)^2\) 32.72
exponential, \(e^{q \cdot k/\tau}\) (usual) 33.98
Gaussian, \(e^{-\lVert q-k\rVert^2/2\tau}\) 34.26

The linear kernel can go negative, so its “weights” are not weights at all and the averages blow up. Any kernel that stays positive and grows with similarity works, and the exponential is within a fraction of a point of the best. The same paper tried tying \(W_Q = W_K\) (a symmetric kernel) and got 33.78, so on this task the symmetry worry cost little. The real reasons the plain exponential stays the default are that it is one matrix multiply and that the speed-ups in part 5 are all built around it.

Why not cosine similarity?

Cosine similarity divides the dot product by both lengths, so every score lands between −1 and 1. That sounds tidy, but it caps how sharp attention can be. In a row of \(n\) words, the best a word can do is score 1 while all the others score −1:

\[p_{max} \le \frac{e^{1}}{e^{1} + (n-1)\,e^{-1}} = \frac{e^2}{e^2 + n - 1}\]

That is at most 60% for our 6 words, and under 1% for 1,000. A head could never focus on one word in a long text. The fix is to multiply the cosines by a learned temperature, which brings back the freedom the dot product had all along. That is QK-norm (Henry et al., 2020). A close cousin, LayerNorm on the queries and keys, kept attention scores from blowing up when training the 22-billion-weight ViT-22B (Dehghani et al., 2023).

Why the softmax, and not something cheaper?

The \(n^2\) cost comes from the softmax. Without it, matrix products can be regrouped:

\[(Q K^\top) V = Q (K^\top V)\]

The left side builds an \(n \times n\) matrix and costs about \(n^2 d_k\). The right side builds a \(d_k \times d_k\) matrix and costs about \(n d_k^2\): linear in \(n\). Linear attention (Katharopoulos et al., 2020) does this, replacing \(e^{q \cdot k}\) with \(\phi(q) \cdot \phi(k)\) for some simple positive function \(\phi\), so the regrouping is allowed.

The price is sharpness. With the softmax, the \(n \times n\) weight matrix can be anything, including close to one-hot rows. With \(\phi\), the score matrix is a product of two thin matrices, so its rank is at most the size of \(\phi\)’s output. Low-rank weights can’t pick out one word among thousands as cleanly. That is one reason the softmax version is still the default.

Attention can’t see order: the proof

Reorder the words with a permutation matrix \(P\): a 0/1 matrix with one 1 in every row and column, so \(PX\) is \(X\) with its rows shuffled. It has the handy property \(P^\top P = I\).

Feed in \(PX\) instead of \(X\). The queries become \(PX W_Q = PQ\), and likewise \(PK\) and \(PV\). The scores become

\[(PQ)(PK)^\top = P\, Q K^\top P^\top\]

which is the old score grid with its rows and its columns shuffled the same way. Softmax works on each row on its own, and doesn’t care about the order of the entries inside a row, so \(\text{softmax}(P S P^\top) = P\, \text{softmax}(S)\, P^\top\). Then

\[P\, \text{softmax}(S)\, P^\top \cdot PV = P\, \text{softmax}(S)\, V = P \cdot \text{Attention}(X)\]

The output is the old output, shuffled. Nothing else changed. Mathematicians call this permutation equivariance, and it is exactly the problem part 2 fixes.

How the gradient flows back

Training needs the gradient of the loss with respect to \(Q\), \(K\) and \(V\). Write \(S = QK^\top / \sqrt{d_k}\), \(P = \text{softmax}(S)\) and \(O = PV\), and let \(dO\) be the gradient arriving at the output. The rules for matrix products give

\[dV = P^\top dO, \qquad dP = dO\, V^\top\]

For the softmax, use the Jacobian from above, one row at a time. For a row \(p\) with incoming gradient \(dp\):

\[ds = \big(\text{diag}(p) - p\,p^\top\big)\, dp = p \odot \big(dp - (p \cdot dp)\big)\]

where \(\odot\) multiplies entry by entry. Then back through the scaled product:

\[dQ = \frac{dS\, K}{\sqrt{d_k}}, \qquad dK = \frac{dS^\top Q}{\sqrt{d_k}}\]

Every gradient to \(Q\) and \(K\) passes through that factor \(p \odot (\cdots)\). In a one-hot row, \(p\) is 0 everywhere except at the winner, and there \(dp - (p \cdot dp)\) is \(dp_{win} - dp_{win} = 0\). So \(ds\) is zero, and \(W_Q\) and \(W_K\) learn nothing from that row: the √d_k story again, seen from the backward pass. \(V\) is different: \(dV = P^\top dO\) has no such factor, so values keep learning either way.

entry.title: how a language model picks the next word

link.title: how a language model picks the next word

entry.content:
You know the word suggestions above your phone keyboard? Type “see you” and it offers “soon”, “tomorrow”, “later”.

A chatbot works the same way, just much better. It never plans a whole answer. It only asks one question, over and over:

Given the text so far, what should come next?

It picks one piece, adds it to the end, and asks again. That’s it. Poems, code and exam answers all come from this one loop.

This post walks through the loop step by step. There are two figures you can play with. Their numbers are a toy I made up by hand, but the steps are the same ones real models use.

The loop

Every reply is built like this:

  1. Read the text so far.
  2. Score every possible next piece. (This is the neural network’s job.)
  3. Turn the scores into chances.
  4. Pick one piece.
  5. Add it to the text, and go back to step 1.

The loop stops when the model picks a special “the end” piece, or runs out of room.

We won’t open up the neural network here. Think of it as a black box that hands us a list of scores.

The pieces are called tokens

I keep saying “piece” because models don’t really use words. They use tokens: chunks of text from a fixed list. Common words are one token. Long or rare words get split up.

The ␣ means “starts with a space”. To the model, ␣cat and cat are two different tokens.

The list of all tokens is the vocabulary. A real one has around 50,000 to 250,000 tokens. For the rest of this post I’ll mostly say “word” anyway, because it’s easier to read.

Step 1: score every word

Take the prompt “The cat sat on the”. The model gives every word in its vocabulary a score. A higher score means “this fits better”. The score has a name, a logit, but it’s just a number.

Scores are hard to read alone. Is 3.1 good? Only if the others are lower. What we want instead are chances: numbers between 0% and 100% that add up to 100%.

Softmax: scores into chances

The tool for this is called softmax. It does two things:

  1. Make every score positive, in a way that stretches out the gaps. (It raises the number e ≈ 2.718 to the power of each score.)
  2. Divide each result by the total, so they add up to 100%.

Here it is with three words:

The best word stays on top, and every word gets some chance. One more useful fact: only the gaps between scores matter. Add 10 to every score and the chances don’t move.

For the curious, the formula is

\[p_i = \frac{e^{z_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{z_j}}\]

where \(z_i\) is the score of word \(i\). You don’t need it for the rest of the post.

Temperature: the “creativity” knob

Many AI tools have a temperature setting. Before softmax, every score is divided by the temperature.

  • Low temperature (below 1) makes the gaps bigger. The favourite wins even more often. Output gets safe and predictable.
  • Temperature 1 leaves the scores as they are.
  • High temperature (above 1) makes the gaps smaller. Unlikely words get more of a chance. Output gets more varied, and sometimes weird.

Notice that mat is always first. Temperature never changes the order. It only changes how far ahead the leader is.

There’s no deep theory behind the “right” temperature. People just try values and see what reads well. Stephen Wolfram, in his ChatGPT essay, found that about 0.8 worked best for essays.

Try it yourself. Drag the temperature slider, then press Pick a word a few times.

Loading interactive figure…

Figure 1. Toy scores for eight possible next words. Model probability is what softmax gives at the current temperature. Sampled counts how often each word came up in your picks. The uncertainty chart shows how unsure the model is at each temperature.

The same eight words at a few temperatures:

Temperature mat floor sofa bed roof keyboard moon banana
0.1 99.8% 0.2% ~0% ~0% ~0% ~0% ~0% ~0%
0.5 65.9% 19.8% 7.3% 4.9% 1.2% 0.8% ~0% ~0%
1.0 41.1% 22.5% 13.7% 11.2% 5.6% 4.6% 1.0% 0.4%
2.0 26.4% 19.5% 15.2% 13.8% 9.7% 8.8% 4.1% 2.5%

At 0.1 the model almost always says mat. At 2.0 it says moon about once in 25 tries.

How unsure is the model?

The “uncertainty” chart in Figure 1 measures how spread out the chances are. It’s called entropy, and it’s counted in bits.

  • 0 bits: one word has all the chance. The model is sure.
  • 3 bits: all eight words are equally likely. That’s as unsure as three coin flips.

Our toy sits at 2.29 bits at temperature 1, and drops to almost 0 at temperature 0.1.

Step 2: pick a word

Now we have chances. We still need to choose one word. The rule for choosing is called the decoding strategy. Here are the common ones.

Greedy: always take the top word. Same prompt, same answer, every time. The downside is that it gets stuck. On long texts it often repeats itself, because once a loop is the most likely path, nothing breaks it out. (Set Figure 1 to top 1 to see greedy.)

Sampling: roll a weighted die. Each word’s chance of coming up equals its probability. At temperature 1, mat comes up about 41% of the time, floor about 22%, and once in a while keyboard. Press Pick 50 times in the figure. The Sampled bars start out bumpy, then slowly match the Model probability bars.

Top-k and top-p: cut off the junk first. A real vocabulary has 100,000+ tokens, and most are nonsense in any given spot. Each is unlikely, but together they add up. So before sampling, we throw most of them away:

  • Top-k keeps only the k best words. Set the figure to top 3 and you get 53.1%, 29.2% and 17.7%, the same three numbers as the softmax example above.
  • Top-p keeps the best words until their chances add up to p, say 90%. At temperature 1 that keeps five words (mat to roof) and drops keyboard, moon and banana.

Top-p is clever because it adapts. When the model is sure, a couple of words already reach 90%. When it’s unsure, more words get in. That’s why many tools use top-p with a medium temperature.

A simple way to remember it: temperature changes how steep the odds are; top-k and top-p change how many words are allowed to play.

Step 3: repeat

Once a word is picked, it joins the text, and the model scores the next spot from scratch. So a whole sentence is a path through a tree of choices.

Click the words below to build your own path, or press Let the model write.

Loading interactive figure…

Figure 2. Each column shows likely next tokens, given everything to their left, with their chance underneath. The highlighted ribbon is your path; thicker lines mean higher chance. ␣ marks a leading space, and "+ others" is the chance left over for every token not shown.

Chances multiply along a path

To get the chance of a whole path, multiply the chance of each step. For the most common path, time → , → there → was:

Even the most popular opening comes out word for word only about 1 time in 7. Each extra word multiplies in another number below 1, so any exact long text is very unlikely.

(Multiplying hundreds of tiny numbers gets so close to zero that computers lose track. So in practice, models add up the logarithms of the chances instead. Same answer, safer maths.)

No going back

A real model has a branch for every token in its vocabulary. With 100,000 tokens, ten steps already give more possible paths than anyone could ever list. So the model never looks at the whole tree. It walks one step at a time, without looking ahead.

That means early choices steer everything after. Pick midnight instead of time in Figure 2 and every later column changes. The model can’t go back and edit an earlier word. It can only keep adding new ones.

What this explains about chatbots

Knowing the loop makes a lot of chatbot behaviour make sense:

  • Same question, different answers. Sampling takes a different path each time. Turn the temperature near 0 and answers become much more repeatable.
  • “Creative” vs “precise” modes. That’s usually just the temperature knob, sometimes with top-p.
  • Repeating itself. Greedy picking and very low temperatures can fall into loops.
  • Confident mistakes. The model picks words that fit, one at a time. Nothing in the loop checks if the whole answer is true. A smooth wrong answer and a smooth right one look the same to it.
  • Wording matters. Your prompt is the start of the path. Change a few words and the very first scores change, and so does everything after.

Summary

  • A model writes by repeating one step: score every token, turn scores into chances, pick one, add it.
  • Softmax turns scores into chances. Only the gaps between scores matter.
  • Temperature makes the odds steeper (low) or flatter (high). It never changes the order.
  • Greedy, sampling, top-k and top-p are different rules for picking.
  • A full reply is a path through a tree. Early picks shape everything after.

Real models do exactly this, just with 100,000+ tokens instead of eight words, and a huge neural network making the scores. How that network works is a story for another post.

Further reading

  • Stephen Wolfram, What Is ChatGPT Doing … and Why Does It Work?: a long, friendly tour of the same loop, with real GPT-2 examples.
  • Maxime Labonne, Decoding Strategies in Large Language Models: greedy, beam search, top-k and top-p, with code.
  • Machine Learning Mastery, How LLMs Choose Their Words: a hands-on walk through logits, softmax and sampling.

The figures are plain JavaScript and SVG: no chart library. The interactive style is inspired by Sophie Wang’s research explainers.
